docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
Give your world a road network: physical roads generated during worldgen that connect its towns and structures, named routes and areas, and map integration that ties it together. Roads are graded, bridged and tunnelled to the terrain they cross, and every settlement they reach is one the game really built.

MC 1.21.1–1.21.11 MC 26.3 Fabric NeoForge No Cobblemon

Get started Commands

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• 🗺️ Dynamic routes between towns and structures, fully part of worldgen — roads are graded to the land, bridge the water, bore through what they cannot climb, share a trunk where they run together, and get names like Route 3: Steep Forest Pass.
  • 🧭 Map integration (optional): waypoints and chunk paint on Xaero's maps and JourneyMap, and waystones named after their towns.
  • 🛣️ Roads by hand: join two towns with the Road Planner and build the road even through land you have already explored.
  • 🧩 World-creation tab: a dedicated ROUTES tab on the create-world screen, with one-click presets for the road network and the road style — every rule set up-front, saved per world, down to the mix of road materials, the bridge decks and the handrails.
  • 🎮 Playing a Pokémon world? With Cobblemon 1.8, route Pokémon live along the roads, and with Radical Cobblemon Trainers, route trainers stand beside them. Cobblemon Nuzlocke & Soul Link is a separate add-on that builds on this one: it locks encounters to the routes, areas and towns generated here, and sets the rules the road trainers follow.

docs.title: Get it
docs.text:
Download Modrinth · CurseForge · What changed Version 2.0.164 Minecraft 1.21.1–1.21.11 · 26.3 Side Server and every player's game Cobblemon Not needed Fabric Fabric API, Architectury API, Cloth Config NeoForge Architectury API, Cloth Config Optional Waystones: each waystone takes the name of the town it stands in · Fabric Waystones: the same, on Fabric · Xaero's Minimap: waypoints and chunk paint on the map · Xaero's World Map: chunk paint on the full-screen map · JourneyMap: waypoints and chunk paint, as on Xaero's · Cobblemon Picnic: about 3 rest stops in 100 are a picnic table · Radical Cobblemon Trainers: route trainers beside the roads · Cobblemon Cities & Structures: its cities are towns of the road network Java 21 for Minecraft 1.21.x, 25 for 26.x Cobblemon 1.8 for route Pokémon along the roads; Routes runs without Cobblemon

New here? Start with Getting Started.

docs.title: ⌨️ Commands
docs.text:
The complete manual for every /routes command — the road network — and for /routesmap, which changes how the map looks to you.

👤 = every player · 🛡️ = operator (permission level 2)

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Command Who One-liner /routes status 👤 How many towns, routes and areas have been discovered. /routes list [cities\|routes] 👤 Every discovered town / route, with coordinates. /routes nearest 👤 Closest discovered town and route, with distance and heading. /routes zone 👤 What the chunk you stand in is painted as. /routes rename <name> 🛡️ Rename the town you are standing in. /routes tp <town> 🛡️ Teleport to a town somebody has visited. /routes remove 🛡️ Remove the town or road you are standing on. /routes zone override <kind> [force] 🛡️ Declare this chunk a different kind, and keep it that way. /routes zone clear [force] 🛡️ Hand this chunk back to the generated map. /routes zone info 🛡️ What the world generated here vs. what the override says. /routes zone create <kind> <from> <to> [name] 🛡️ Author a whole box as a named zone. /routes zone expand\|reduce <name> <from> <to> 🛡️ Grow or shrink it by a box. /routes zone delete\|rename <name> … 🛡️ Remove it, or rename it. /routes zone list 🛡️ Every authored zone: kind, chunks, author. Laburo (item) 🛡️ The same zone authoring, by clicking two corners. No recipe — creative only. /routes settlement … 🛡️ Your own towns and connections in the road network. /routes road preview\|commit\|cancel 🛡️ Build a declared road into land that is already generated. /routes road tool 🛡️ Hands you the Road Planner: click one town, then the other. /routes config … 👤/🛡️ Read and change this world's settings from in game. /routes debug … 🛡️ Sixteen reports, for pasting into a bug report. Three of them change the world. /routesmap … 👤 How the chunk paint looks on your own map. Never reaches the server.

docs.title: 🛤️ /routes — the road network
docs.text: status, list and nearest answer from what players have discovered — the towns somebody has walked into, the routes somebody has walked, the areas somebody has entered — never from the whole world the seed has planned. Until someone has, they answer Nothing discovered yet — walk into a town or onto a road first. The whole planned network is what debug towns, further down, is for.

docs.title: status — 👤
docs.text: The world at a glance: how many towns, routes and areas have been discovered.

docs.title: list [cities|routes] — 👤
docs.text: The full inventory. cities lists every discovered town with its x, z coordinates; routes lists every discovered route — Route 7: Something — with its two towns. With no argument you get both. Long lists are capped at 24 lines with an "… and N more" trailer.

docs.title: nearest — 👤
docs.text: Where's civilization? Reports the closest discovered town and the closest discovered route to where you stand, each with the distance in blocks and a compass heading (N, NE, E, …). Great when you're lost in open wilderness.

docs.title: rename <name> — 🛡️
docs.text: Renames the town you are standing in, generated or declared. The new name reaches the arrival banner, /routes list, the map marker and the signs: the ones already standing are rewritten as their chunks load. Two towns can't share a name.

docs.title: tp <town> — 🛡️
docs.text: Teleports you to a town somebody has visited — tab-completion suggests each one — landing on a safe, dry column: the same spot-finder that places a new world's spawn. Wrong name? It points you at /routes list cities.

docs.title: 🗺️ zone — what the ground under you is
zone — 👤
docs.text: The map-paint (and capture-zone) debugger: tells you what the chunk you are standing in is painted as — a CITY (with its name), a ROUTE (name and endpoints), an enclosed AREA (its A#-Name, or unnamed until first entered), or open wilderness (unpainted until your network encloses it). Always agrees with the map colours and the zone pop-ups.

docs.title: zone override <kind> [force] — 🛡️
docs.text:
Declares the chunk you are standing in to be a different kind, and keeps it that way. The map, the pop-ups and /routes zone all follow the override from then on.

Kind The chunk is city part of a town road part of a route on open ground cave part of a route where it runs through a tunnel bridge part of a route where it crosses on a bridge — over a river or a dry gap aquatic part of a route across open water, too wide to bridge subaquatic part of a route along a seabed. Roads no longer generate this way; the kind stays so older chunks that carry it can still be authored none nothing at all — the way to take a town or a road off a chunk

There is no area kind: an area is the space the mod finds between the painted chunks, so it follows from the roads around it.

Overrides are a second layer over the generated map, not an edit of it: the underlying paint is untouched, so a chunk you clear falls back to whatever the world generated. Tab-completion offers the valid kinds.

force overrides a chunk that already carries one.

docs.title: zone clear [force] — 🛡️
docs.text: Removes the override on this chunk, handing it back to the generated map. force clears one you did not author.

docs.title: zone info — 🛡️
docs.text: Prints both answers side by side for this chunk: what the world generated, and what the override says. The first stop when the map and /routes zone disagree with each other.

docs.title: zone create <kind> <from> <to> [name] [force] — 🛡️
docs.text:
Authors every chunk of a box as one kind, under a name you can manage it by afterwards. The two corners are ordinary coordinates and accept ~ ~, so the usual way to draw one is to stand at a corner and type ~ ~, walk to the opposite corner, and type ~ ~ again.

Leave the name out and it gets a generic one — Z1, Z2, … — which you can change later with zone rename. force comes after the name, so a zone you want to force needs one: /routes zone create road ~ ~ ~20 ~20 Pass force.

The box is capped at 1024 chunks (32 × 32). A box over the cap does nothing at all rather than half of it; build bigger zones in pieces with zone expand.

docs.title: zone expand <name> <from> <to> [force] — 🛡️
docs.text: Adds a box to a zone that already exists. The kind comes from the zone itself, not from you — a zone with two kinds in it would not be one zone.

docs.title: zone reduce <name> <from> <to> — 🛡️
docs.text: Takes a box back out of that zone. Only chunks of that zone are touched, so a box that overspills onto a neighbour leaves the neighbour alone — which is why this one needs no force.

docs.title: zone delete <name> [force] — 🛡️
docs.text: Hands every chunk of the zone back to the generator. force is needed only for chunks somebody else authored.

docs.title: zone rename <name> <newName> — 🛡️
docs.text: Renames it, and re-marks it under the new name. The old marker stays on the map until you rejoin — Xaero owns runtime waypoints and this mod cannot take one back off, so every zone is re-sent from its current name and centre when you join.

docs.title: zone list — 🛡️
docs.text:
Every authored zone: name, kind, how many chunks, and who authored it. Also counts the one-off overrides from zone override, which belong to no zone.

Authoring a zone does not build anything

These commands decide what ground counts as — for the map, for the zone pop-ups, and for the capture zones of Cobblemon Nuzlocke & Soul Link. They do not put a road in the ground: roads are drawn as terrain generates, so authoring a route across country you have already explored gives you a route on the map with no road under it.

Reassignment is refused on purpose

A chunk that already belongs to something is refused, and the report names what it would have taken. That is not caution for its own sake: a chunk's zone is the capture zone, so moving one from one zone to another can retroactively change whether a catch already made there was legal. force goes through anyway, and the report tells you exactly what it overwrote.

docs.title: 🔴 The Laburo — the same thing, by hand
docs.text:
A red-bladed shovel for map makers. It does the same write the commands above do, but you point at the corners instead of typing them.

It has no recipe. Take it from the Tools tab of the creative inventory, or /give it. It does nothing at all without operator permission, so a crafting recipe would only put it in a survival player's hands and teach them it is broken.

Do this And it Right-click a block sets one corner — then the opposite corner, which creates the zone Sneak + right-click changes what the next zone will be: town → road → nothing Right-click the air tells you the mode, and forgets a corner you left pending

The new zone gets a generic name (Z1, Z2, …) — rename it with /routes zone rename <name> <newName>.

An authored zone gets its own marker

A town or a road that the world generated is named from the road network, so its marker comes from there. A zone you drew is not in that network — it is named after itself. Its marker carries the zone's own name (Z1, or whatever you renamed it to), sits at the middle of it, and comes back every time you rejoin.

Why there is no area mode

An area is not something you paint. It is the enclosed space the mod finds between the painted chunks, so the way to make one is to author the roads that enclose it.

The tool never forces

Where the box crosses ground that already belongs to something, those chunks are left alone and the tool names what stood in the way. There is no gesture for overriding that on purpose — /routes zone expand <name> <from> <to> force is, and it stays typed.

docs.title: 🟩 Areas close themselves
docs.text:
You never draw an area. An area is the space left between the roads, so the way to make one is to enclose it — and the moment an authoring edit closes a pocket, that pocket is named and marked, and whatever you used to close it tells you how many appeared.

That works the same whether you closed the ring with /routes zone create, with expand, or with the Laburo. Areas that close the ordinary way, as the world generates its own roads, are unchanged.

A pocket has to be a reasonable size to count: too small and it is a road curving back on itself, too large and it is simply open country.

An area is not un-named if you open it again

Take away the roads that enclosed an area and the ground opens up, but the area keeps its name and its marker. That is deliberate and it is the same rule every other record here follows: it is the register of what somebody has already seen, and in a Nuzlocke world catches are counted against it. Quietly retiring one would move a capture zone out from under a catch already made.

docs.title: 🏘️ settlement — your own towns and connections
docs.text:
These feed the settlement graph — the network that draws roads as the world generates — exactly as if the world had put those towns and roads there itself.

Declared settlements and connections, and everything removed or withdrawn, are remembered with the world and survive a restart. Every removal here only affects chunks generated from now on: ground already generated keeps what was built on it.

docs.title: remove — 🛡️
docs.text: Removes whatever you are standing on. In a town it removes the town, exactly as settlement remove does. On a road it withdraws that road, and names it — Route 7: Ashvale ↔ Mirefield. The road is the one actually drawn through your chunk, so standing in the middle of a route is enough, with neither of its towns in sight. If two roads run through the chunk, it lists them and removes nothing; walk to where only one does. Right after loading, the roads nearby may still be planning; it says so, and asking again a moment later works. settlement reconnect puts a road back.

docs.title: settlement add [name] — 🛡️
docs.text: Registers where you are standing as a settlement in the gen2 graph, optionally named. Roads plan to it as if the world had generated a town there.

docs.title: settlement remove — 🛡️
docs.text: Removes the settlement nearest to you. One you declared is deleted. One the world generated is taken out of the network, along with every road it carried.

docs.title: settlement restore — 🛡️
docs.text: Puts back the nearest generated town you removed, exactly as it was: its name and its roads. A settlement you declared cannot be restored, because settlement remove deletes it: declare it again with settlement add.

docs.title: settlement list — 🛡️
docs.text: Every settlement and connection you have declared in this world, with coordinates.

docs.title: settlement connect <x> <z> — 🛡️
docs.text:
Declares a road between the town nearest to you and the one nearest to x, z. Either end can be a settlement you declared or a town the world generated: each end is the declared settlement near it or, where there is none, the nearest generated town. A declared connection is the one edge nothing is allowed to re-route: it exists because you said those two places are joined.

Like everything here it reaches chunks generated from now on. For land you have already explored between the two towns, follow it with road preview and road commit.

docs.title: settlement disconnect <x> <z> — 🛡️
docs.text: Takes the road between the town you stand at and the one nearest x, z out of the network. A road you declared is deleted. A road the world generated is withdrawn, and both towns keep their other roads.

docs.title: settlement reconnect [<x> <z>] — 🛡️
docs.text: Puts a withdrawn road back. With no position, it restores the road withdrawn most recently, which is the only way to bring back a branch that starts at a fork. With a position, it restores the road between the town you stand at and the one nearest x, z.

docs.title: 🛣️ road — a road through land already explored
docs.text: A declared connection only reaches chunks generated after it, which does nothing for the ground between two towns you have already walked. These commands draw it there too.

docs.title: road preview — 🛡️
docs.text: Plans the connection you declared last and shows its line as a trail of particles over the ground near you, with its length, its two ends and how many chunks it crosses. Ground an add-on has claimed (a gym, a building) is counted and left untouched.

docs.title: road commit — 🛡️
docs.text: Draws the previewed road into the world, chunks already generated included. One commit draws into at most 600 chunks; a longer road does nothing at all, rather than half of it. Signposts and rest stops come with chunks generated from then on.

docs.title: road cancel — 🛡️
docs.text: Drops the preview. The declared connection stays.

docs.title: road tool — 🛡️ — the Road Planner
docs.text:
Hands you the Road Planner, the same thing by hand:

Do this And it Right-click the ground at one town sets the first end Right-click the ground at the other declares the road and previews it, ready for /routes road commit Sneak + right-click clears the first end

Either town can be a generated one or one you declared. Clicking two towns that are already joined previews the road between them.

docs.title: ⚙️ config — read and change this world's settings
docs.text:
The whole tree is generated from the same option catalog the world-creation tabs are built from, so every setting on the ROUTES tab is reachable here, and neither surface can drift from the other. See World Creation & Config for what each one does.

An option is named by its key, not by its label on the tab: Road width is route_width. config list prints every key next to its value, and tab-completion offers them.

A change is written twice: onto the settings the game is reading right now, and into the rules stored with the world — so it takes effect immediately and survives the next load.

docs.title: config list — 👤
docs.text: Every option and its current value, grouped under the same six headings the ROUTES tab uses.

docs.title: config get <option> — 👤
docs.text: One option and its current value.

docs.title: config set <option> <value> — 🛡️
docs.text:
Changes it. The value is typed: a number option only accepts a number within its own limits, a toggle only accepts true/false, and an option with a fixed set of choices tab-completes them. A list option is typed as a, b, c, and a material mix as minecraft:cobblestone=70,minecraft:gravel=30.

A setting that shapes the road network is fixed for each world: setting one saves it for the worlds you create next, says so, and leaves this world's network as it is.

docs.title: config reset <option> — 🛡️
docs.text:
Back to the mod's own default for that option.

Some settings only affect ground that has not generated yet

Anything about the shape of the road network — how many roads leave a town, how long they may be, how steep, how wide — decides what gets built. Changing it does not rebuild what is already there. See the note on each option in Configuration.

docs.title: 🎨 /routesmap — how your map looks
docs.text:
A separate command from /routes, because it answers a different question: not what the world is, but how the chunk paint looks on your map. It runs entirely in your own game — it never reaches the server — so every player can use it, with no operator rights, on any server, including one that has never heard of Routes.

Changes show on the minimap and the world map the moment you press Enter, and are still yours after rejoining.

Command What it does /routesmap opens a small screen with every setting below — changes apply as you make them, with the map still in view /routesmap list prints every setting at once /routesmap paint on\|off the chunk paint on both maps /routesmap opacity city\|route\|area <0-100> how strong that category's tint is; 0 hides it /routesmap colour city\|route\|area <colour> that category's colour: magenta, orange, teal, red, green, blue, yellow or white /routesmap waypoints per_category\|all_in_one one waypoint set per category, so each can be hidden on its own — or one set for the whole mod, so a single switch hides them all /routesmap waypoints custom [name] every waypoint goes into the set (or JourneyMap group) with that name; use the name of one of your own sets to mix them in. Without a name it keeps the last one, Routes at first /routesmap waypoints off Routes adds no waypoints to Xaero's maps or JourneyMap, and shows no Waypoint discovered toast

A colour drives the tint and the matching waypoints together, so the map and its markers always agree; the waypoints take it on your next join. A new grouping re-files each waypoint as you rediscover it.

docs.title: 🔬 debug — measure it instead of guessing
docs.text:
Operator tooling, and it prints raw English rather than translated text: it exists to be pasted into a bug report.

Three of them change the world

debug paint, debug areas and debug spawn are not reports. They write to the world you run them in, and nothing undoes them. Run them on a copy, never on a world you care about. The rest only read.

Most take a radius in chunks and default to something sensible, so /routes debug gaps on its own is usually what you want.

Command Radius What it reports debug towns [r] 8–512, def. 128 every settlement the seed puts in range, as the road network sees them debug settlements [r] 8–256, def. 64 the settlement graph with a census: how many roads each rule contributed, and how many were folded into shared trunks. The answer to "why does this world have so many roads" debug graph [r] 8–512, def. 128 the graph's nodes and how they cluster debug edges [r] 8–512, def. 128 every planned road in range, with its endpoints debug paint [r] 1–32, def. 8 ⚠️ draws the planned roads into the chunks around you that are already generated, and paints them on the map, then says how many chunks it touched debug areas [r] 1–48, def. 16 ⚠️ places a sponge on top of every enclosed-area chunk in range, so you can see where the areas are debug verify [r] 8–512, def. 128 walks the roads in range and reports anything that does not add up debug gaps [r] 8–512, def. 128 measured on the road as it was really laid (climb ladders skipped, a slab or a slab next to a stair counted as half a block, the road read under eaves and ledges, a tunnel ramp read off its own blocks; a village's own terraces and houses are not judged): every place a road, a tunnel or a bridge hands over to the next, and the size of the step there; a step of two blocks or more says whether it has a ladder, and if not why (too tall, at a bridge or tunnel, on a chunk border…). Where a "the road has a hole in it" report starts debug bridge [r] 8–512, def. 128 walks each bridge span and reports cells with no deck, with coordinates debug bore [r] 8–512, def. 128 what stands in the way inside each tunnel in range: every block id that would stop a walker (read on the floor you actually walk on, also where the tunnel climbs), with how many and where the first one is. The first few blocks at each end belong to the entrance ramp and are counted apart as hand-over columns; whether the step from the ramp into the tunnel is walkable is what debug verify measures. Where a "the tunnel is blocked" report starts debug forks [r] 8–512, def. 128 the ground around each fork in range, flattest last, and how many of its signposts are standing debug step — for the column you stand on and its four neighbours: the height the road was planned at, the real ground, the height the road is actually built at, and whether it got a slab, a full block or a stair, and why. Tells a badly planned step from one the builder had to cut short debug spawn — ⚠️ moves the world spawn: runs the spawn finder again, puts the spawn in the town it picks, and says why debug workers — where the background road work has spent its time: tasks, waits, and work done that nothing used debug bench [columns] 16–10000, def. 400 times the road drawer over that many columns debug chunks [count] [away] 4–4096, def. 64 times whole chunk generation, optionally away blocks from you so it measures cold ground

What to paste into a report

For a road that looks wrong: debug gaps and, if a bridge or a tunnel is involved, debug bridge or debug bore. For a town that should be connected and is not: debug towns and debug settlements. For anything slow: debug chunks and debug workers.

Commands of the classic generator

scan, connect, addcity, delcity, weave, repaint, reset and debug structures belonged to the road generator Routes retired in 2.0, and are gone. Use /routes settlement add, settlement remove and settlement connect instead.

docs.title: 🧩 World Creation & Config
docs.text:
Everything is decided when you create the world — a dedicated ROUTES tab sits next to GAME / WORLD / MORE on the create-world screen. Outside world creation there's a global config screen for defaults, opened from the mod list (Mod Menu on Fabric, the Config button on NeoForge).

Looking for the NUZLOCKE tab?

The Nuzlocke ruleset, its starter options and the Soul Link toggles belong to Cobblemon Nuzlocke & Soul Link — install that add-on and its tab appears next to this one.

  1. Set on the ROUTES tab when you create the world
  2. Defaults from the global config (key K, config/routes.json) for a world that was not configured
  3. Result your world's rules, saved with that world and never overwritten later

docs.title: ROUTES tab
docs.text: Two rows of presets open the tab, then the options sit in six sections, in the order you meet them: where roads go, how they look, how they get past hills and water, what they do near landmarks, where you start, and an Advanced section at the end. Advanced starts closed; once you open or close it, it stays that way for the rest of the session. The Mod Menu config screen shows the same sections.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
Row Choices What it sets Road network Sparse · Balanced · Dense Roads per town, longest road and ring roads. Sparse: 2 roads per town, none longer than 1000 blocks, no ring roads. Balanced: 4, up to 1600, with ring roads. Dense: 5, up to 2400, with ring roads Road style Trails · Roads · Highways Road width, winding, lamp posts, tunnel size and wear. Trails: 3 wide, winding, worn, no lamp posts, small tunnels. Roads: 5 wide, lamp posts on some roads. Highways: 7 wide, nearly straight, lamp posts on every road, big tunnels

Balanced and Roads are the defaults. Change one of those options by hand and its row shows Custom.

docs.title: Where roads go
docs.text: Option Default Notes Build roads between towns on master switch. Off: no roads planned, and the spawn stays where the game puts it Roads per town 4 1–5, a ceiling, not a count: each town rolls its own up to this, inside the band its size puts it in (a village low, a city high), so the network has hamlets and crossroads Longest road (blocks) 1600 the farthest two towns can be and still get a direct road Ring roads on keep closing loops between towns that are close on the map but far apart by road. Loops are what enclose named areas Bigger towns get more roads on settlements come as village, town or city by their real footprint, and a bigger one carries more roads. Needs Check towns before building roads Towns & landmarks automatic every structure your world has, each set to Town, Landmark, Ignored or Underground town, with a Reset to Routes' list button on top. See Which structures get roads

docs.title: How roads look
docs.text: Option Default Notes Road surface Random (by biome) Random paves each stretch from the palette of the biome it crosses, so a road changes material where the land changes. Pick one material, or press + Add material to mix several: each row has a Share slider (70 and 30 pave about 70% and 30%), laid in rounded patches. Random (by biome) can be one entry of the mix. See Road materials Road wear 0% 0–30: that share of a road's flat blocks is laid as a worn version of its material: cracked or mossy stone bricks, gravel in cobblestone, grass through a dirt path. Stairs never wear Road width 5 3–9, odd numbers; the brush is symmetric around the centreline How much roads wind 5 0 = ruler-straight, 10 = follows every fold of the land Bridge deck Random (by biome) Random builds each bridge from the timber of its biome. Pick one plank or a mix: each bridge takes one of them for its whole span, and its stairs follow the same wood Handrail Random (per route) Random gives each route one of twelve fences and walls. Pick one or a mix: each route takes one for its whole length Lamp posts Random Random / On / Off. Random decides per route Tunnel lanterns Random Random keeps some tunnels as dark caves Lights along water crossings Random a sea lantern in the pillar under each water-crossing marker. Random decides per route Road names on Route 3: Steep Pass on signposts, waypoints and zone banners; off keeps the plain Route 3. Roads already numbered keep their name Picnic stops 3 with Cobblemon Picnic installed, the percent of rest stops that are a picnic table instead of a camp. 0 = never, 100 = every stop Route Pokémon on with Cobblemon 1.8 installed, wild Pokémon appear along the roads (see Dynamic Routes). Off adds no new spots; the ones already there stay

docs.title: Road materials
docs.text:
The Road surface picker offers these materials. Each one paves every road in that block; Random (by biome) is the default.

Choice Block Random (by biome) random — the biome palette below Dirt Path minecraft:dirt_path Cobblestone minecraft:cobblestone Mossy Cobblestone minecraft:mossy_cobblestone Gravel minecraft:gravel Stone Bricks minecraft:stone_bricks Mossy Stone Bricks minecraft:mossy_stone_bricks Cracked Stone Bricks minecraft:cracked_stone_bricks Andesite minecraft:andesite Polished Andesite minecraft:polished_andesite Sandstone minecraft:sandstone Cut Sandstone minecraft:cut_sandstone Cut Red Sandstone minecraft:cut_red_sandstone Packed Mud minecraft:packed_mud Mud Bricks minecraft:mud_bricks Coarse Dirt minecraft:coarse_dirt

A mix holds up to six of them. In the config file or with /routes config set path_block_material, the setting also takes any other block id, modded ones included, as minecraft:cobblestone=70,minecraft:gravel=30. An id the game does not know is dropped from the mix, and if nothing is left the road falls back to Random.

What Random lays. Each stretch takes its block from the biome it crosses, in patches a few blocks across. The biome's name is checked first, then its temperature:

Biome Random draws from Badlands cobblestone, cut red sandstone, gravel, stone bricks Swamp, mangrove swamp packed mud, mud bricks, mossy cobblestone, coarse dirt Jungle mossy cobblestone, mossy stone bricks, dirt path, gravel Desert, beach, very hot biomes cobblestone, cut sandstone, gravel, stone bricks Frozen stone bricks, cobblestone, cracked stone bricks, gravel Cold cobblestone, stone bricks, andesite, gravel Temperate dirt path, cobblestone, mossy cobblestone, stone bricks, gravel Warm dirt path, packed mud, sandstone, gravel

Bridge deck offers oak, spruce, birch, jungle, acacia, dark oak, mangrove, cherry, bamboo, crimson and warped planks; the config file takes any planks block. Random uses the biome's timber: cherry in a cherry grove, mangrove in a mangrove swamp, bamboo in a bamboo jungle, dark oak in a dark forest or badlands, birch in a birch forest, jungle in a jungle, acacia in a savanna, spruce in taiga, mountains and the cold, oak everywhere else.

Handrail offers oak, spruce, birch, jungle, acacia, dark oak, mangrove and cherry fences, and cobblestone, mossy cobblestone, stone brick, mossy stone brick, andesite and diorite walls; the config file takes any fence or wall. Random rolls one of twelve per route: every fence but mangrove and cherry, and the six walls.

docs.title: Hills, rivers and tunnels
docs.text:
Option Default Notes Steepest climb 8 1–10, tenths of a block per block. Higher lets roads climb steeper hills; lower makes them cut through or tunnel instead Dig tunnels on off, a planned tunnel is built as a steep surface road over the top Tunnel width 9 a tunnel's own width, twice the road's. Only the bore widens; the ramp down to it stays road-width. Odd numbers, like the road Tunnel height 8 floor to ceiling. Taller tunnels leave a thinner roof in low hills Build bridges on off, a river becomes an open water lane and a dry gap is followed on the ground Bridges run straight across on a bridge over water runs straight from bank to bank however much the road winds; off, the crossing weaves with the road. A bridge over a dry gap weaves either way Water crossing width 10 the marked lane across a lake or sea. Its own number, not a multiple of the road: open water reads much wider than it is Steps at tunnel mouths on the ramp out of a tunnel starts with a stair off the tunnel floor, never a step of a block and a half Tunnels surface before a town on a road that would reach a town inside a tunnel comes up before the first building and enters on the surface, by the street, with its welcome sign. The ground under a town is never dug. Roads that already arrive on the surface keep their shape. Fixed per world Smooth diagonal road steps on a road climbing on the diagonal gets no step of a block and a half at its corners: that column is lifted half a block, unless it would leave a step of more than a block on its other side Smooth fork edges on a road leaves a fork's levelled ground without a wall at its edge, and no paving or slab is left hanging over air beside it Roads sharing ground agree on its height on where roads run together into a fork, over the same strip or side by side, that ground is laid at the lowest of their heights and a road beside another comes down to meet it by half a block per block, so there are no walls between them. Off, each road keeps its own height and the last one drawn wins No road scraps inside towns on a road starts after the last building or street of the town it leaves, however far apart two of them are. Off, only gaps of up to ten blocks are left to the town, so a longer one can keep a short piece of road ending in a wall Enter CCS towns by their streets on a road into a town of Cobblemon Cities & Structures joins the end of a street the town left open, the one facing the road, and not the side of a street or an empty house lot. Does nothing in vanilla villages, in other town packs, or without that mod Bridge ramps meet the road on the ramp up to a bridge always reaches the road below at one step, never a wall, even under a high deck: it steepens over its last cells to hand over to the road Ladders on walls at chunk borders on a wall of two blocks or more where a road crosses into the next chunk, as on a tunnel ramp, gets a ladder like any other wall. Off, such a wall is laddered only if the planned road already stepped there No slab that leaves a step and a half on a slab smooths a one-block rise only where it leaves no step of a block and a half beside it, on the diagonal or into the next chunk; there the rise takes a stair instead

The nine look-and-fit options in that list (everything from Steps at tunnel mouths down, except Tunnels surface before a town) only change chunks generated from now on: roads already in your world keep their blocks, and the planned routes do not move. Tunnels surface before a town reshapes the planned road, so it follows the rule below for settings that shape the network.

docs.title: Landmarks
docs.text: Option Default Notes Roads go around landmarks on a road steers around a landmark's (or an ignored structure's) real footprint instead of cutting through it; where one fills the only way through, the road is still built Roads pass by one landmark 3 0–10: how strongly a road bends to pass beside the one landmark it visits, a few blocks and never a detour. 0 = off How far a road detours (blocks) 96 how far off a road's straight line a landmark can be and still pull it Sign the landmark a road passes on a signpost beside the road names the landmark it passes Landmark waypoints on the first time you walk past the landmark a road signs, it gets a waypoint on your map, in its own Landmarks set. See Map Integration Waystones take the town's name on with Waystones or Fabric Waystones installed, a waystone takes the name of its town the first time it is activated or discovered; a name you give it afterwards stays. Off: Routes never renames a waystone. See Map Integration

docs.title: Your first steps
docs.text: Option Default Notes Start in a town on move a new world's spawn into the nearest town; off leaves the vanilla wilderness spawn. Only a world being created does this: a world you already had keeps its spawn when Routes arrives (/routes debug spawn moves it by hand) Prepare the land around spawn 512 chunks built in the background the first time you enter, so the roads and towns around spawn are already built when you walk out. The default reaches the spawn town and its first road, about 200 blocks. 0 = off

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
Ten options a first world rarely needs. The section starts closed.

Option Default Notes Every surface structure gets roads off also connect surface structures that are not towns, never one whose id names a ruin, an ancient thing or a mineshaft Routes' structure list on the hand-reviewed list of towns, landmarks and structures to ignore that ships with Routes (gym entrances included). Your own choices in Towns & landmarks always beat it. See Which structures get roads Town ids only empty exact structure ids that count as towns. Empty = the automatic rule Never start in RS ocean village towns that may never be the world's first town. They stay ordinary towns otherwise Check towns before building roads on check the town really generates before the network sends a road to it, so no road ends at an empty field Town size (blocks) 64 blocks across from which a settlement is a town rather than a village City size (blocks) 128 blocks across from which it is a city. /routes debug settlements shows how your world's towns fall into the three Shape the land with the road on the ground is road-shaped before anything is planted on it, instead of cut and filled afterwards. Decided once, when the world is created Build road chunks early on generate a road's chunks a little before you reach them, so the cost lands while you walk Area names on A3-Frostpine on an area's waypoint and banner; off keeps the plain Area 3

docs.title: Map & Notifications (not on the tab)
docs.text:
Zone notifications (Off / Toast / Announcement / Chat: how entering a route or an area is announced) and Map chunk paint (on: tint chunks on Xaero's maps and JourneyMap by category) are your own preferences, not world rules, so they are not on the create-world tab. Set them in Routes' config screen (Mod Menu on Fabric, the Config button on NeoForge), under Map & Notifications; the chunk paint, the tint intensity, the colours and the waypoints are also changed in play with /routesmap, with the map in front of you.

Routes builds the towns and the roads between them, and with Radical Cobblemon Trainers installed it also places the route trainers beside the roads (see Dynamic Routes). The gyms next to towns, the league and the Nuzlocke rules belong to Cobblemon Nuzlocke & Soul Link, on its NUZLOCKE tab.

Saved per world, and some fixed for good

Choices made in these tabs are stored per world and only applied to a brand-new world: loading an existing world never gets its rules clobbered. Confirming them says World rules set: ….

The settings that shape the road network stay at the value the world was created with: roads per town, longest road, ring roads, bigger towns get more roads, the towns & landmarks list, road width, how much roads wind, picnic stops, steepest climb, bridges run straight across, tunnels surface before a town, the three landmark-path settings (go around, pass by, how far), and in Advanced every surface structure gets roads, Routes' structure list, town ids only, check towns and the town and city sizes. Changing one mid-world would give the land generated afterwards a second network whose roads stop short of the old ones. /routes config set on one of them saves the value for the worlds you create next and says so; /routes config list marks them.

docs.title: Global defaults
docs.text: The global defaults live in config/routes.json (English & Spanish labels) and are used when a world wasn't configured through the tabs. The map-paint intensity and colours are changed in play with /routesmap.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: The root is /routes (the old /cobblemonroutes alias is gone). The full manual — every command, argument, permission and behaviour — lives on the Commands page.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Routes runs on Minecraft 1.21.1 to 1.21.11 and 26.3, on Fabric and NeoForge.

  1. 1 Download the jar for your loader and Minecraft version
  2. 2 Drop it into mods/
  3. 3 Launch the game
  4. 4 Create a new world and open the ROUTES tab

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Dependency Notes Minecraft 1.21.1–1.21.11 or 26.3, each with its own jar Java 21 for 1.21.x, 25 for 26.x Fabric Loader or NeoForge the one your Minecraft version uses Fabric API Fabric only Architectury API both loaders Cloth Config bundles AutoConfig

Optional but integrated: Waystones, Fabric Waystones, Xaero's Minimap / World Map and JourneyMap (see Map Integration), Cobblemon Picnic (picnic tables at rest stops), Cobblemon 1.8 (route Pokémon along the roads), Radical Cobblemon Trainers (route trainers beside the roads) and Cobblemon Cities & Structures (its cities get roads). See Dynamic Routes.

The mod does not bundle these — install them alongside it.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Download the version matching your loader and your Minecraft version from Modrinth or CurseForge. The file names say both: routes-fabric-2.0.145+1.21.1.jar is the Fabric jar for 1.21.1. One jar covers a group of versions and is named after the newest of them: +1.21.3 runs on 1.21.2 and 1.21.3, +1.21.8 on 1.21.6 to 1.21.8, +1.21.10 on 1.21.9 and 1.21.10. For 26.x only 26.3 has a jar; 2.0.86 was the last version for 26.1.x and 26.2.
  2. Drop the jar into your profile's mods/ folder.
  3. Make sure only one routes-*.jar is present (remove older ones first).
  4. Launch. Create a new world and look for the ROUTES tab on the create-world screen.

New save recommended

Route rules are chosen at world creation and stored per world, and the road network is laid out as the world generates. Starting a fresh world gives you the intended experience.

Updating a world from Minecraft 1.21.x to 26.x

Minecraft 26.1 moves a world's saved data into a new folder. Routes picks up its own files from the old place on the first start, so the roads, the map paint, the zones and the world's rules come along.

docs.title: 🧭 Map Integration
docs.text:
Routes talks to the maps you already use. Everything on this page is optional — the mod detects what's installed and stays inert otherwise.

Map mod What Routes adds 🪨 Waystones · Fabric Waystones A waystone takes the name of the town it stands in 🧭 Xaero's Minimap Waypoints and toasts, chunk paint 🗾 Xaero's World Map (key M) Chunk paint 🗺️ JourneyMap Waypoints in their own groups, chunk paint

docs.title: Waystones
docs.text:
Activating a waystone names it after the Routes town it stands in and counts as a visit to that town — your fast-travel points carry the same names as the places the roads connect.

Fabric Waystones (Wraith Waystones; Fabric only — that mod has no NeoForge version) is supported too. A waystone takes the name of the Routes town it stands in the moment you discover it, and shares that town's map marker, so the waystone, the town and the pin are one place under one name.

Routes names a waystone only once, the first time it sees it. If you rename the waystone afterwards, your name stays. To keep Routes from renaming waystones at all, turn off Waystones take the town's name (/routes config set route_waystone_names false).

docs.title: Xaero's Minimap
docs.text:
• Auto waypoints — the first time you reach a named town, a route or an enclosed area, it drops a pin with a toast; every named waystone you activate does the same. Unnamed places are ignored, and a marker never doubles up — Xaero forgets runtime waypoints when you relog, so they are re-sent on join and de-duplicated on arrival. An Underground town's marker sits at the town's own depth, not on the ground above it.
  • Landmark waypoints — the landmark a road passes (the one its roadside sign names) gets a pin the first time you walk that stretch of road, in its own Landmarks set. Turn it off with Landmark waypoints in Configuration.
  • Where the waypoints go — one set for the whole mod, one per category, a set you name (use one of your own sets to mix them in with your waypoints), or off: no waypoints and no Waypoint discovered toast. Chosen with /routesmap.
  • Chunk paint 🎨 — the xaero_chunk_paint option (default on) tints chunks on the map by category, with a subtle low-opacity wash: magenta over cities/villages, orange over routes, and teal over an area once it is fully enclosed by your cities and routes — open wilderness stays unpainted until the network grows around it. Enclosed areas earn a name (A1, A2, … with a nature flavour, e.g. "A3-Frostpine") shown by their entry pop-up.

Chunks are painted once your map has discovered them, so a new world's map is not tinted far from anywhere you have been.

docs.title: Xaero's World Map
docs.text: The chunk paint also renders on the full-screen World Map (key M) — visible independently of the minimap's Cave Mode and of your Y level, on the surface and in caves alike.

docs.title: JourneyMap
docs.text: JourneyMap gets the same chunk paint and the same waypoints as Xaero's maps, in the same colours. JourneyMap's unit for hiding a set of markers is a waypoint group, so each category gets a group named like the Xaero set — Settlements, Routes, Areas and Landmarks — or one Routes Mod (all) group under the single-switch grouping, or the group you name. The markers are re-sent every time you join, so nothing of Routes stays in your JourneyMap data if you remove the mod. They always go on the Overworld map, even if you join in the Nether.

docs.title: Changing how it looks — /routesmap
docs.text:
How the paint looks (on Xaero's maps and JourneyMap alike) is a choice about your own map, so it is a command every player can use: no operator rights, and it works on any server — even one without Routes — because it never leaves your game. It turns the paint on and off, sets how strong each of the three tints is (0 hides that category), picks each one's colour — which the matching waypoints follow — and chooses where the waypoints land: one set, one per category, a set you name, or nowhere.

Type /routesmap on its own and a small screen opens over the world with all of it: drag a slider and the minimap behind it re-tints as you go. Each setting is also a subcommand, for anyone who would rather type it. Your choices are still there after rejoining.

To hide and show the paint with one key, bind Show / hide chunk paint under Routes in Options → Controls → Key Binds. It ships unbound, so it never fights Xaero's own keys. Every argument is on the Commands page.

Note

Get the map mods from Xaero's Minimap, JourneyMap and Waystones — then everything above just works.

docs.title: 🗺️ Dynamic Routes
docs.text:
Routes grows a road network through your world during worldgen — no commands, no walking the area first. Cities are found from the world seed, connected with terrain-aware paths, and every road is signposted and named.

steep mountain in the way

water in the way

🔍 Locate cities from the seedvillages · modpack towns · gym entrances

🧠 Terrain-aware pathfindingprefers flat, inland ground

⛏️ Bore a mineshaft tunnel~⅓ are dark caves — bring a torch!

🌊 Water crossingbridge deck or open lane between rock markers

🛤️ Build the roadnatural palette + lamp posts

🪧 Signs at ends & junctionsname · destination · distance

✨ Route 3: Steep Forest Pass

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Automatic road network between cities — vanilla villages, modpack villages, the gym entrances of the packs Routes ships a list for, and any structure you list. Built incrementally and resumed after a restart.
  • Flat & inland paths — the pathfinder strongly penalises slopes and keeps a buffer away from shorelines, while still crossing water when there's no alternative.
  • Mineshaft tunnels — when a climb is too steep (or there's no surface path at all), the route bores a clean, walkable, oak-framed tunnel — twice the road's width and eight blocks tall — instead of an impassable cliff. About a third of tunnels are atmospheric dark caves — bring torches!
  • Descriptive route names — every road gets a code plus an auto-generated name from the terrain it crosses (Route 5: Coastal Road, Route 8: Marsh Crossing), always the same for your seed.
  • Clean tree clearing — a road crossing a tree removes the whole trunk and canopy; no floating leaves, no item spam. Trees and huge mushrooms don't grow within a few blocks of the road's edge, so no crown hangs over the road where you walk. Any leaves or branches a tree hangs into the 3 blocks above a road, including the strip right at its edge, are trimmed away; the forest beside it is left.
  • Water crossings — always on the surface. A river gets a plank bridge with its pillars dropped to the riverbed, in one wood from end to end; a longer stretch stays an open lane of water to swim or sail, marked on both edges by natural rock markers, most of them lit, and the road meets it at the shore's own height. The seabed is never touched, and a frozen lake keeps its ice. Water the planner could not see coming (a river carved later by Streams Reflowing, an aquifer pool) is crossed on a timber bridge at the banks' height, not left as a swim gap. With Streams Reflowing installed, roads keep off its river banks and cross its rivers squarely.
  • Bridges on real supports — the posts under a bridge's edges are full logs of the bridge's own wood, with a log beam across under the deck at every post row.
  • Climbs you can walk — a road that climbs steps up in half blocks (slab, full block, slab), in the road's own material: it starts a climb a few blocks early and finishes it a few blocks late, so up to four rises in a row are walked in slabs. Only a longer climb keeps a stair, where the slabs run out. Every one-block step gets a stair or a slab, on the ramps up to a bridge, into a tunnel and out of a town too; a bridge deck that rises one block takes a slab. A wall that is still two blocks or more gets a ladder, whichever way you walk in. Where a road reaches a bridge ramp half a block low, both blocks are stairs, so there is no wall to jump. The ramp out of a tunnel starts with a stair off the tunnel floor, and a road climbing on the diagonal has no corner a block and a half high: a slab smooths a rise only where it leaves no such step beside it, on the diagonal or into the next chunk, and otherwise the rise takes a stair. The ramp up to a bridge reaches the road below at one step, never a wall, and a wall of two blocks or more where a road crosses into the next chunk gets its ladder too.
  • Roads made of what you choose — the surface can be one material or a mix laid in rounded patches, with an optional share of worn blocks (cracked or mossy bricks, gravel in cobblestone, grass through a dirt path). Bridge decks and handrails are chosen the same way, one material per bridge and per route. Left on Random, each stretch takes the palette of the biome it crosses. See Configuration.
  • Signs everywhere — directional signs at each end and at junctions (one per road, even at a fork right by a chunk border), with plaza-paved crossings that stand out from the road, and a welcome board with the town's name where a road arrives.
  • Junctions built for the spot — where two roads cross, the crossing is either a ringed roundabout around a lit pillar or an open signed crossing with fingerposts naming all four destinations. Roads that meet at different heights are an overpass: the upper one simply bridges over. A fork that lands inside a hill opens into a chamber where its tunnels meet, with its signposts on the chamber floor beside the roads. On a hillside the ground around a fork is levelled for its signposts, and each road stays level across it and starts to climb at its edge, with no wall at the rim and no paving left over air beside it. Roads that run together into a fork share the same ground at one height, the lowest of theirs, with no steps between one road and the next. A road's signpost is not put where another road runs.
  • Rest stops — every few hundred blocks, a small camp just off the road: a campfire with log seats, a lantern post and a sign. Now and then one keeps a supply chest from the last traveller — rarely, so finding one still means something. With Cobblemon Picnic installed, now and then a stop is one of its picnic tables instead — about 3 in 100, set by Picnic stops in Configuration.
  • Landmarks along the way — a road passing a pyramid, a tower or a ruin bends a little to go by it, keeps off its footprint, and puts up a signpost with its name. No road is planned to a landmark — see Which structures get roads.
  • Villages, towns and cities — a settlement's real size decides how many roads leave it, so the network has quiet hamlets and busy hubs. A fork out of a big town stands past its last houses, never among them. A road ends where a village really ends: a leftover scrap of road between two houses or streets is left as the village's own ground, however far apart they are. A road that would reach a town inside a tunnel comes up to the surface before the first building and enters by the street. A structure tagged routes:settlement/village, routes:settlement/town or routes:settlement/city gets that word after its name, so Pallet becomes Pallet Town. The cities of Cobblemon Cities & Structures (Pewter, Cerulean, Vermilion, Celadon, Fuchsia, Saffron, Cinnabar and Viridian, plus Lavender and Pallet when placed by hand) are towns of the network too: a road joins the end of a street those towns left open, the one facing it, and Routes still works without that mod.
  • Underground towns — any structure can be set as an Underground town in Which structures get roads. Its road ends at the surface, and right beside the end a stone-brick spiral stairway goes down to the town: slab half-steps, a landing every 8 blocks down, a short tunnel at the bottom, and a ↓ town board at the top naming the town below. Two underground towns are never joined directly; each is reached from a town on the surface. Nothing is set this way by default.
  • Route Pokémon — with Cobblemon 1.8 installed, roads carry habitat blocks hidden in the paving, each spawning its own Pokémon family at its own level band, leaning toward the biome's natives (Water types by water crossings, Flying types on bridges). No legendaries, Ultra Beasts, Paradox Pokémon or starters. Turn them off with Route Pokémon in Configuration.
  • Route trainers — with Radical Cobblemon Trainers installed, a trainer stands beside the road every 160 blocks as you explore it, with a team near your party's level, and swimmers at water spots. No gym leaders, Elite Four or Champions. Without RCT nothing changes.
  • Roads meet the town's own streets — a road joins a town at the open end of a street, at street level, never behind a house or climbing into the air. A pack can mark its street ends with an open jigsaw named routes:city_exit, and the road then continues the street that faces it most squarely.
  • Spawn in a city — new worlds start next to the nearest city, on real ground, never in the water — coastal towns included.
  • A loading screen that shows the real wait — while a new world opens, two towns and the road between them are the progress bar. Each step (surveying the towns around your spawn, generating the spawn chunks, building your spawn town) gets its share of the road by how long it really takes. The road's tip only moves while work actually finishes, the line under it counts tasks done, and it says no progress for N s when nothing has finished for a while. Until you are in the world the survey uses every processor core but one, and goes back to four once you are playing; the towns and roads of a seed are the same either way.

Tune it per world

How many roads, how they look, materials, lighting and more are all set from the ROUTES tab at world creation, with one-click Road network and Road style presets on top — see World Creation & Config.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common surprises, what causes them, and what to do. If yours is not here, post it in the Discord: it files the ticket for you.

docs.title: The game will not start and names a mod
docs.text: Routes needs Architectury API and Cloth Config on both loaders, and Fabric API on Fabric. The loader names the one that is missing. The full list is in the table at the bottom of the home page.

docs.title: I changed a setting and the roads did not change
docs.text: Anything about the shape of the network (how many roads leave a town, how long they may be, how steep, how wide) decides what gets built. It applies to ground that has not generated yet, and never rebuilds what is already there. Each option says so in Configuration.

docs.title: Routes in a world I already had
docs.text:
Route rules are chosen when the world is created and stored with it, and the road network is laid out as the world generates. A new world gives you the intended experience; see Getting Started. To join two towns in land you have already explored, use /routes road.

A world made with the classic generator (Routes 0.77.0 or 1.0.0, or one where the old use_gen2 setting was turned off by hand) is no longer supported: the roads already built stay in the world, but it loses its old map paint, zone banners and town and route names, and new chunks get today's roads like any other world.

docs.title: A town I expected is not connected
docs.text: Routes only connects the structures it finds in your world, and it decides that per kind of structure. See Which Structures Get Roads. If one still looks wrong, the next section says what to send.

docs.title: What to paste into a report
docs.text: For a road that looks wrong: /routes debug gaps and, if a bridge or a tunnel is involved, /routes debug bridge or /routes debug bore. For a town that should be connected and is not: /routes debug towns and /routes debug settlements. For anything slow: /routes debug chunks and /routes debug workers. See Commands.

docs.title: 🏘️ Which structures get roads
docs.text:
Every structure in your world is one of four things to the road network:

What it is What the roads do Town a village, a town, a city roads are planned to it Landmark somewhere worth seeing — a pyramid, a ruin, a tower no road is planned to it; a road passing near it bends a little to go by it, keeps off its footprint, and signs it Ignored underground, at sea, or not in the Overworld not visited and not signed; a road still goes around one that stands on the surface, as it does around a landmark Underground town a town built under the ground a road runs to the spot above it, and a stone spiral stairway beside the road's end goes down to it

Routes decides each one for you, and for most worlds its answer is the one you want. When it is not, the three recipes below change it: one for a new world, one for a world you already play, and one for pack authors.

docs.title: Make a structure a town, a landmark or ignored
When you create a world: the ROUTES tab
docs.text:
1. On the create-world screen, open the ROUTES tab.
  2. Under Where roads go, click ▶ Towns & landmarks to unfold the structure list. It holds every structure your world will have, from every mod and data pack you installed.
  3. Find your structure. The list is grouped by the mod it comes from, one bold heading per mod: Minecraft first, then the others in alphabetical order of their mod id. Inside a group the towns come first, then Other structures, each in alphabetical order. A row is named from the structure's id (minecraft:village_plains reads Village Plains); hover a row to see the id itself.
  4. Click the row's button until it reads what you want: Town → Landmark → Ignored → Underground town, and round again.

That is all: the world is created with your choice. Reset to Routes' list, at the top of the structure list, puts every row back to Routes' own answer.

Finding the id of a structure you have seen in game

Type /locate structure in any world with the same mods and let tab-completion list the ids. The part before the : is the mod id, which is the heading to look under.

docs.title: On a world you already play
docs.text:
A structure's role cannot change in a world that already has roads. The world records the structure list the moment its first roads are planned, so that every chunk generated later belongs to the same network: a change halfway through would leave roads ending at a seam. What you can do in that world, as an operator:

  • Make one structure a town: stand in it and run /routes settlement add [name]. Roads plan to it as if the world had generated a town there.
  • Take one town off the network: stand near it and run /routes settlement remove. Its roads go with it; /routes settlement restore brings both back.

See the settlement commands for the rest.

To change the list for the worlds you create next, /routes config set writes it into your own config, which the ROUTES tab starts from:

/routes config set route_city_structure_tags minecraft:village, bca:villages, -minecraft:village_desert
/routes config set route_landmark_structure_tags mymod:old_tower

set replaces the whole list, so type every entry you want to keep, separated by commas. Run /routes config get route_city_structure_tags first to see what is in it. The grammar is in the structure lists.

docs.title: For a pack author: a data pack
docs.text:
Routes reads three structure tags, and a data pack can add to any of them:

Tag File in your data pack routes:settlements data/routes/tags/worldgen/structure/settlements.json routes:landmarks data/routes/tags/worldgen/structure/landmarks.json routes:ignored data/routes/tags/worldgen/structure/ignored.json

This one makes a mod's camp a town and its ruined tower a landmark:

data/routes/tags/worldgen/structure/settlements.json
{
  "replace": false,
  "values": [
    { "id": "mymod:camp", "required": false }
  ]
}
data/routes/tags/worldgen/structure/landmarks.json
{
  "replace": false,
  "values": [
    { "id": "mymod:ruined_tower", "required": false }
  ]
}
  • "replace": false adds to what Routes ships. "replace": true throws Routes' list for that tag away and keeps only yours.
  • "required": false keeps the tag loading when the mod that owns the structure is not installed.
  • A structure belongs in one of the three. One listed in two is read in this order: routes:ignored first, then routes:settlements, then routes:landmarks.
  • There is no tag for Underground town: that one is only set from the ROUTES tab or the config.

Add the data pack before you create the world. Added to a world that already has roads, it changes only the ground not generated yet, and the roads there may not meet the ones built before. It is read below the player's own choices, so a row someone changes on the ROUTES tab beats it, and it is read only while Routes' structure list (under Advanced) is on.

docs.title: Check that it worked
docs.text:
• A town: run /locate structure <id>, go there, and run /routes debug towns (operator). It lists the towns the road network knows around you, nearest first, with their coordinates; yours is the one at the coordinates /locate gave.
  • A landmark: follow a road that passes near it — within How far a road detours, 96 blocks unless you changed it. The road bends to go by it, and a signpost beside the road names it.
  • Ignored: no road goes to it, and none signs it.
  • Underground town: a road ends near the spot above it, beside a stairway going down.

docs.title: What a road does beside a landmark
docs.text:
• It goes around it. The road steers clear of the structure's real footprint, never through the middle of a ruin. Where a landmark fills the only way through, the road still gets built.
  • It passes by it. A landmark close to where a road is heading pulls the road over a few blocks so you walk past it. A road visits at most one, the one nearest its line, so roads don't zigzag.
  • It signs it. Where the road passes, a signpost beside it names the landmark. A structure from a mod the sign doesn't know is named from its id, so it still reads as a name.

Each of the three has its own option under Landmarks on the ROUTES tab: Roads go around landmarks, Roads pass by one landmark and Sign the landmark a road passes.

docs.title: The list Routes ships
docs.text:
Routes comes with its own answer for the structures of the packs it is tested on — which are towns, which are landmarks and which to ignore — so a pack like the Cobblemon Official Modpack gets roads to its gym entrances with no config at all, and the Kanto cities of Cobblemon Cities & Structures are towns. It is the three structure tags of the data-pack recipe, shipped in the jar.

It sits below everything you choose: a row you change on the ROUTES tab, and every entry of the lists below, beats it. A structure it does not name is decided by the automatic rule. Turn it off with Routes' structure list, under Advanced on the ROUTES tab.

docs.title: The structure lists
docs.text:
The ROUTES tab rows write three lists in the config, and /routes config and config/routes.json edit the same lists by hand:

  • route_city_structure_tags — what counts as a town;
  • route_landmark_structure_tags — what counts as a landmark, among the things that are not towns;
  • route_underground_structure_tags — what is an Underground town. Inclusions only.

The first two have the same grammar, and both add to the automatic rule rather than replacing it:

You write It means minecraft:village_plains this exact structure is one #bca:villages every structure in that tag is one -minecraft:village_desert this one is not, whatever anything else says -#minecraft:village nothing in that tag is

The - prefix is what a row writes when you move it off a role, and it is read before everything else — so an exclusion always wins, including over the built-in rule that says a village is a town. A structure excluded from both lists is Ignored.

docs.title: Advanced options
docs.text: Three options under Advanced on the ROUTES tab change how the whole list is decided. A first world needs none of them.

docs.title: Town ids only
docs.text:
Town ids only (gen2_settlement_allowlist) is different from everything above: the moment it holds a single id, it is the whole truth about towns. Only the ids in it are towns, the automatic rule stops applying, and route_city_structure_tags is not consulted at all.

It is all-or-nothing, and that is the point

Put one gym in it and your world's villages stop getting roads. Leave it empty — the default — unless you want to hand-author the complete list yourself.

docs.title: Every surface structure gets roads
docs.text:
Every surface structure gets roads (connect_all_structures) is the opposite extreme: every surface structure becomes a town. Underground ones are still skipped, so roads do not dive for a mineshaft.

It makes for a very dense network. It is there for map makers and for seeing what a pack contains.

docs.title: Routes' structure list
docs.text: On by default. Off, Routes ignores the list it ships and guesses every structure you have not set yourself from its name.

docs.title: The order things are decided in
docs.text:
Routes first asks "is this an Underground town?": only a structure you set to one is, and that answer beats every rule below. Then it asks "is this a town?", and stops at the first rule that answers:

  1. Town ids only, if it has anything in it — that is the whole answer.
  2. Every surface structure gets roads, if it is on — every surface structure is one.
  3. Your town exclusions — anything you wrote with a -, or moved off Town.
  4. The village rule — anything in the #minecraft:village tag.
  5. Your town inclusions — the ids and tags you added.
  6. The list Routes ships — a town it names is one, and a landmark or an ignored structure it names is not, whatever its id says.
  7. The name rule — an id that calls itself a village, a town or a city.

Anything that is not a town then gets the second question — landmark or ignored:

  1. Your landmark exclusions — Ignored.
  2. Your landmark inclusions — Landmark.
  3. The list Routes ships — a landmark or an ignored structure it names.
  4. Otherwise it is a Landmark, unless it is not in the Overworld, every biome it can generate in is ocean, or its name says it is built underground — a mineshaft, a stronghold, a dungeon, a buried or sunken thing, an ancient city, trial chambers. Those are Ignored.

The reason exclusions sit above the village rule is so moving a village off Town actually works: without that, the village rule would answer first and the change would do nothing.

To see which towns these rules gave a world, run /routes debug towns in it.

docs.title: A note for pack authors
docs.text:
A road is planned to a town's street layout, not to a point — the connector walks the road tip to the nearest real street piece and hands over there. A structure with no streets still gets a road, it just meets it at the edge. A road joins at the open end of a street, at the street's own height, never at a leftover connector behind a building.

  • Choose where roads come in. Mark a street end with an open jigsaw named routes:city_exit and a road into the town ends on one of those exits — the one facing it most squarely — so it continues your street. Exits no road uses stay ordinary dead-end streets.
  • Say what kind of place it is. Tag the structure routes:settlement/village, routes:settlement/town or routes:settlement/city and its name gets that word: Pallet becomes Pallet Town. A name that already ends in one (Black City) is left as it is.

Structures that only exist in the Nether or the End are never connected: roads are an Overworld thing.
